Business.title: Meet the gen Zers finding job opportunities teaching English abroad
Business.text:
A year ago, Arianna Marie, 25, was struggling to control the students in her Florida elementary school classroom.

She was living with her parents to save on rent and quickly feeling her passion for teaching dry up, even though it was her first job since graduation.

“I was extremely burnt out,” Marie said. “We had a teacher shortage, so all of my classes were overcrowded.”

When her district wanted to transfer her to a new school, she looked for opportunities abroad. Through an English-language teaching job in South Korea, Marie is now living in Daegu, a city in the south-eastern part of the country, with enough pay and benefits that she can save and travel.

The fact that it’s the home to K-pop and K-dramas doesn’t hurt – and in a striking shift, she’s rediscovered her love for the job. “I never have to crack down on behavior issues, and both students and teachers respect me so much,” Marie said. “I actually get to focus solely on teaching.”

Marie is part of a program by the South Korean government that is placing native English speakers with a college degree and Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) certificates with local public schools, as it increases spending on education. Benefits include free housing, flight reimbursements, healthcare and monthly salaries starting at about $1,400.

Graduating with a college degree in the US no longer comes with the stability it once guaranteed. Since the Covid pandemic, the unemployment rate for recent college graduates has been higher than the overall unemployment rate.

For those who have a job, earnings have been rising slower than the pace of inflation. New entrants in US public service jobs like teaching are increasingly leaving the profession, citing low pay and high stress.

Other countries, including Japan and Taiwan, are similarly investing in full-time English-language teachers, attracting young workers with benefits they would be hard-pressed to find in their home countries.

Gen Z is spreading the word. Some English-language teachers have garnered thousands of followers on TikTok and Instagram, showing audiences their lives abroad. Marie has been keeping track of her travels, and documenting some of her classroom experiences, on her Instagram account.

The TEFL Institute, which issues TEFL certification courses that accredit English-language teachers, notes that the English-language teaching market was valued at $95bn in 2026, with more than 2m TEFL jobs available worldwide. The market is expected to reach $181bn by 2034, and the Asia-Pacific region is growing the fastest.

As the US federal government has gutted the Department of Education, American public school teachers, who are overwhelmingly female, are especially feeling the pull to overseas jobs.

But the phenomenon isn’t exclusive to Americans, or teachers. Zwiwe Dlamini, 28, was spiraling into a deep depression working as an administrative assistant in Durban, South Africa.

“I’ve always been behind the desk, gathering minutes, gathering meetings, working for CEOs and it was just extremely draining,” Dlamini said.

Though she knew that finding a better job at home would be difficult – the youth unemployment rate in South Africa is notoriously high, at almost 70% – Dlamini still quit her job. After six months of job searching, she knew she would have to look elsewhere.

After she applied to the same program as Marie, she ended up in Incheon, the north-west South Korean city, as an English-language teacher. The free housing and low monthly expenses have allowed her to start paying off her debt while having enough savings to travel and plan for a master’s degree.

“One year ago, [I] could not have imagined the position I am in today,” Dlamini said. “I couldn’t afford food and had [accumulated] debt, so paying it off now and still [experiencing] life to the fullest – I am actually so grateful.”

John Bentley, co-founder of the International TEFL Academy, which offers TEFL certification courses, noted that interest in teaching English abroad particularly soared after the 2024 presidential election.

“With a difficult political and economic situation, we see gen Z turning to TEFL,” he said. “A lot of people go with the intention of staying for just one year. What happens is they fall in love with the country or experience and stay three [or] four years, or even much longer.”

This tracks with a broader trend of Americans who increasingly say that they want to migrate. Last year, a Gallup poll found that 40% of US women said they would move abroad if given the chance.

Marie said her South Korean classroom, which she shares with another teacher, is worlds apart from her former classroom in Florida, where she would handle more than 20 kids on her own.

“We always say that teaching is extremely undervalued in the US, but here you can tell how much they do value it,” she said. “The students are more receptive when I correct them and have so much respect for me as a teacher.”

Business.title: ‘If it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it’: Canadians on boycotting Trump’s America
Business.text:
For William McDonald, 38, a diesel mechanic from Thunder Bay, Ontario, “Canadian is always the first choice,” even if it means his weekly bills are higher.

“As soon as Trump started putting those tariffs on in February [last year], I started boycotting US goods,” he said. “Avoiding American products has driven my costs up, and I’m still happy to do it.

“I used to drink US beer, but now I drink Canadian beer, and that costs me an extra C$1,000 (£531/US$720) a year. Likewise, groceries cost about C$50 more a week, but you work that extra hour to pay for it.”

McDonald likened Donald Trump’s behaviour towards Canada as “a lot like the schoolyard bully yelling and stomping their feet when they don’t get the cowering reaction they expect”.

This week the US imposed 50% tariffs on US$20bn (£15bn) of Canadian goods, and Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar” after the collapse of trade talks between the two countries last weekend. Donald Trump retaliated on Thursday by ordering the federal government to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Such actions have added fuel to a widespread boycott of US products and services by Canadians that began early last year in response to the president’s trade war and threats to annex his northern neighbour.

More than 3,500 people from across Canada shared with the Guardian via an online callout how they have made changes to their lives in response to the US administration’s political and economic stance. Many expressed deep anger and sadness, but remained resolute that this was now a new way of living.

Buying only Canadian groceries, including fresh produce, and boycotting travel south of the border featured heavily among the responses. Respondents have stopped paying for US technology; streaming services provided by Netflix, AmazonPrime, AppleTV and Disney+; petrol; vehicles such as Teslas; and whiskies including Jack Daniel’s. Social media sites including X, Facebook and Instagram were also being avoided.

In July, an Angus Reid survey found 40% of grocery shoppers were actively checking where products came from, and most of those avoiding US products where possible.

The ABUS (Anything but US) or ABUSA (Anywhere but USA) acronyms and “Elbows Up!” slogan – a hockey term for offering a stiff defence – began appearing in Canada last year.

“I think you need to be in Canada to understand how deep the animosity to the US is … even across the political spectrum,” said Denise from Winnipeg, Manitoba.

“‘Elbows up’ is a real thing. We don’t fly US airlines, we stay in locally owned hotels, we won’t even connect in a US airport … we’ve moved investments to Canadian companies, and we actively avoid USA products, produce and groceries. It can be pretty inconvenient to do the research and read signs and labels, and often more costly, but BDS [boycott, divestment, sanction] is the only tool ordinary people have to stand up for our values.”

Elizabeth Lorenz, 68, a retired teacher who lives in Nanaimo, British Columbia, said she would change a recipe to work around a lack of certain ingredients.

“I read labels on packaged food, and if it’s made in the US, I don’t buy it,” she said. “Annie’s Pasta is an example of a product I no longer purchase.

“Grocery stores are increasingly offering more produce from Mexico, Peru, Guatemala, Chile and South Africa. Although this means the transportation of this produce has contributed to more environmental degradation than if I were to buy American produce, my outrage at America’s greed and corruption trumps (apologies for the pun) my environmental concerns.”

She has planted yams and sweet potatoes in her garden “since only American-grown yams and sweet potatoes are available”, she said.

Jane, 54, a teacher, was one of many who believed the relationship between the US and Canada had been badly damaged, perhaps beyond repair.

“I definitely will not support America economically while this administration is in power and, to be honest, I may not ever again,” she said.

“The relationship, in my eyes, has been permanently tarnished.”

Jane has been buying only Canadian groceries and alcohol for more than a year and has also stopped travelling to the US, opting for a longer journey to see sports in Canada.

“I have been vacationing in Mexico and the Dominican Republic and Europe instead,” said Jane, who lives in Camlachie, Ontario. “I used to go to Detroit for sporting events or concerts and would pick up gas and groceries before returning to Canada. For more than a year, I have been driving four hours to Toronto for those events that I normally would drive only an hour to in the US.”

She said at first making the changes to non-US goods was “quite challenging” but she uses apps and online forums which direct her to Canadian options.

Among the many US products Jane has replaced with Canadian equivalents are Heinz Tomato Ketchup, Kraft Cheese and Charmin toilet paper. She uses the apps CanMade – Canadian Made, Buy Beaver and O SCANada: Buy Canadian. She also uses the website madeinca.ca.

“Grocery shopping is now easier as stickers are used to indicate place of origin,” she said. “Checking origin of product information has become second nature to me now.”

The same is true of James Buchan, 36, who works in IT, lives in Halifax, Nova Scotia and describes himself as “a habitual label reader”.

“All Procter & Gamble and Colgate products have been replaced by Attitude and Lavo products from Quebec,” he said.

“Canadian produce is quite easy to get hold of, and we can get food from Mexico, but ready-made meals are more difficult to find, as the US has it on lock. So making the change could be more difficult for some.”

He also did a clearout of his tech. “I sold all my Apple products: a year-old MacBook, iPhone, AirTags and AirPods, and replaced them with alternatives,” he said. “Tech was the easiest – I do not miss my iPhone or Mac at all.”

He switched his email providers to European-based ones and has done the same for his mapping applications, language-learning apps and calendar. He also left Facebook, Reddit, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Kurt, 61, a retired engineer who lives in Calgary, Alberta, said his whiskey-tasting group “spent a small fortune” annually on American whiskies – in the region of US$10,000.

“Since ‘Liberation Day’ and the first round of tariffs, we decided one way of expressing our distaste is not to buy American whiskies,” he said. “So since then we’ve spent US$0.00. Amazingly, we just stumbled on a whole new batch of Canadian equivalents. We didn’t realise the range and quality of stuff available locally. So we’ve got no intention of ever going back.”

He is also now a “vigorous” label checker, but added this was not always straightforward, citing the US company Kraft, which has a Canadian operation, employs Canadians, and “uses Canadian materials and ingredients when they can”.

“It actually pains me to buy a product that, yes, it’s made here in Canada, but we know their revenues are going back to the company in the States,” he said.

His wife also no longer drinks California wine, and despite being “frequent visitors for 30-plus years” to the US, Kurt said they have not been there since January 2025.

Many who got in touch with the Guardian felt that trust had been broken irrevocably with their US neighbour.

“I won’t go back to buying US products, even if the regime changes, because the US is unreliable and untrustworthy,” said Sarika, 61, an academic who lives in Vancouver.

“It’s a shame, as many of us in the border regions have friends across the border, and we don’t want to see their businesses and towns suffer, but perhaps Americans will now get a little more involved in voting for and enabling a more fair and just government and trade system.”

Vikram, 51, who works at a finance firm and lives in Toronto, said he refused to travel to the US even though he has family there. They visit him instead. He also avoids US products and is now boycotting Amazon.

He reflected the sentiment of many who found the turn of events lamentable.

“I find it quite sad that Canadians are forced to do this as a protest against these ridiculous threats to our sovereignty, but I’m not sure how else to react,” he said. “We cannot go back to looking at our relationship with the US as it was before, because things have changed. We need to shift focus for our own protection and to maintain our sovereignty and control over our economy.”

Kurt, however, sounded a quiet note of optimism.

“We’re going to look back, and we’re going to say, you know what, it was painful, and it was a shock, especially to have your best friend turn on you, but it was the best thing that could ever happen to us,” he said. “Canada will be stronger and healthier after all this is over.”

William also took some solace from how he feels things have changed in Canada.

“After years of internal division in our country, it’s nice to finally see something bind us together again,” he said. “I guess sometimes it just takes a mutual enemy to find one’s resolve.”

Business.title: Fed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persists
Business.text:
The US Federal Reserve is not done fighting high inflation, its chair, Kevin Warsh, said in his first major speech in the role on Friday, emphasizing that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”.

Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. But his speech was taken by markets as a signal that rates may rise in the coming months, a move that may put him at odds with Donald Trump, who has aggressively called for rates to be cut.

The Fed chair painted a rosy view of the economy that contrasts with recent data. He said the economy “appears to have strengthened” given how it has held up to shocks.

“On that score, both Main Street and Wall Street have been resilient,” Warsh said at the Fed’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday.

The Jackson Hole symposium has typically served as a platform for Fed chairs to offer clarity on the central bank’s general direction. For example, former Fed chair Jerome Powell foreshadowed rate cuts at his keynote address last year.

But Warsh on Friday insisted the days of such “forward guidance” were over, saying that the practice was adopted by the Fed during the 2008 financial crisis. “As with other legacies of crises past, I believe that the practice has overstayed its welcome,” he said.

Markets are still expected to carefully gauge Warsh’s speech for signs of the Fed’s next move. At the central bank’s last board meeting in July, three out of 12 voting members wanted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point – the first time in a decade so many board members shared dissent over a policy position. But a majority of the members voted to hold rates, which currently sit at a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, steady.

Since he was appointed in May, Warsh has had to strike a delicate balance between managing an economy that has been shaken by higher oil prices brought on by the war in Iran without provoking the ire of the White House. Trump has continued to insist the Fed should lower interest rates, despite economists who warn that that would further exacerbate inflation. After hitting a three-year high of 4.2% in May, US inflation cooled to 3.4% in July – still 1% higher than figures seen last year.

Warsh said progress on inflation over the past several years has been “modest”, and though price readings from over the summer came in better than expected, they did not indicate that “underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.

The US bond market has been particularly sensitive to higher inflation, with the yield on 10-year notes hitting its highest level since 2007 in recent weeks. Yields briefly went down after the US treasury announced a big debt buy-back scheme, though the relief proved to be temporary. Rising rates in the US have driven yields higher abroad – bond rates in the UK, Germany, France and Japan have all hit their highest levels in decades. Meanwhile, the US gross national debt topped $40tn for the first time in history last week.

In reaction to Warsh’s opening remarks, the two-year and 10-year US treasury yields increased slightly, while the 30-year treasury remained largely the same. The S&P 500 remained leveled while the Dow Jones ticked down slightly.

Business.title: Ex-Barclays boss denies having sex with woman dressed as Snow White after Epstein emails
Business.text:
The former Barclays boss Jes Staley has denied having sex with a woman dressed as Snow White, after being questioned about an infamous email exchange about Disney princesses with Jeffrey Epstein.

The comments were detailed in newly released transcripts from a closed-door interview last month with US lawmakers as part of their investigation into Epstein, who died in prison in August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

In the email exchange on 9 and 10 July 2010 Staley and Epstein referred to Disney princesses. In those messages, the details of which have been circulating in the media since 2021, Staley tells Epstein: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.”

Epstein then asks: “What character would you like next?” to which Staley replied: “Beauty and the Beast.” Epstein responded: “Well one side is availble [sic].”

During his congressional testimony, Staley, who spent more than three decades at JPMorgan Chase before joining Barclays in 2015, was asked: “Did you ever have sex with a young woman in a Snow White costume?

“No, I did not,” Staley said.

Lawmakers then questioned Staley about another email, sent to Epstein by an unnamed individual on 10 July 2010 and which said: “the snow white was f..ed twice as soon as she put her costume))”. Epstein appears to have asked an unnamed individual to buy a Snow White costume weeks before those exchanges, on 20 June 2010.

“Why would this young woman have sent this email to Mr. Epstein if the two of you had not had sex while she was wearing a Snow White costume and if Mr. Epstein had not instructed her to do so?” a congressional representative, whose name has been redacted from the transcript, asked.

“I have no idea who else she was with. I – it has nothing to do with me, though,” Staley said. When pressed further, he said: “I may have seen her in apartment [sic] and prompted that email. But I was not with a person dressed as Snow White outside of potentially crossing at his apartment.”

The representative asked: “So you may have seen her in his apartment, later emailed Mr. Epstein and said, ‘That was fun,’ but it was not because you had sex with her?”

“That’s correct,” Staley said.

In the transcript, Staley is then asked: “Would you agree that’s a pretty incredible coincidence, that you email him on July 9th, saying, ‘That was fun, say hi to Snow White,’ and then [the unnamed individual] emails him the next day, reporting back on something that just didn’t have anything to do with you?”

“Sure. Why not?” Staley said.

“That’s pretty hard to believe,” the representative said.

The former banker was also asked whether he and Epstein used “Disney princesses as code names for selecting women for sexual encounters”, to which Staley replied, “No.”

Staley’s reputation has been tarnished as a result of his well-documented friendship with the child sex offender.

Staley originally met Epstein in 2000 after he became head of JP Morgan’s private bank, where Epstein was a client. Staley later took over as chief executive of Barclays, one of the UK’s largest banks, in 2015 but was forced to step down in 2021 after City regulators opened an investigation into his relationship with Epstein.

Business.title: CEOs earn 614 times more than workers at US’s 100 lowest-paying corporations
Business.text:
The average CEO of the US’s 100 largest, lowest-paying corporations earned 614 times more than their average worker last year, according to an analysis by the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS).

IPS’s latest executive excess report analyzed compensation at the 100 S&P 500 corporations with the lowest median worker pay. Between 2019 and 2025, CEO compensation increased 41.4%, unadjusted for inflation, twice as much as the median worker pay increased at these firms during the same period, at 20.7%.

Inflation also outpaced worker pay increases, rising by 25.9%.

The CEO-to-worker pay ratio at the low-wage 100 firms increased 8.4% between 2019 and 2025.

The average CEO compensation among low-wage 100 corporations was $17.5m in 2025, compared with median worker pay of $36,571.

The wealth of at least 36 billionaires is linked to these low-wage 100 corporations, including Walmart’s eight Walton family members, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott, and Carvana co-founders Ernie Garcia II and Ernie Garcia III.

“This is really a big problem for society, that we have such extremes,” said Sarah Anderson, lead author of the report and director of the Global Economy Project at the Institute for Policy Studies.

“To me, it seems like these CEOs are just living on a remote economic planet from the one that their employees are living on, and it makes it really hard for them to fathom what it’s like to have to worry about putting food on your family’s table or even coming home at night if you are at risk of being detained by ICE.”

The report notes that the low-wage 100 corporations have a combined force of 1,282 registered federal lobbyists and that many of these companies did not denounce aggressive immigration enforcement actions toward their workforce or on their property.

“Low-wage workers are now facing the biggest cuts to Medicaid and Snap [food benefits] in history. Many of the employees at these companies have to rely on those programs, and then so many of them have also been terrorized and detained by ICE agents,” added Anderson. “So it’s really astounding that the leaders of these companies have turned a blind eye to this surge of threats against many of their workers, and instead they’ve just continue to be fixated on enriching themselves.”

Stock buybacks among these firms increased in 2025, to $108.6bn from $105bn in 2024. Between 2019 and 2025, the low-wage 100 firms spent $718bn on stock buybacks.

Among the 100 low-wage firms, Walmart spent the most on stock buybacks, at $8.1bn, equivalent to a $3,851 bonus to each of the company’s 2.1 million workers. Walmart’s CEO, Doug McMillan, who stepped down in January 2026, received $29.2m in compensation in 2025, 958 times more than the median worker pay at Walmart of $30,520.

The report cites several policy solutions to excessive executive pay at corporations, including a tax hike on corporations that pay CEOs more than 50 times what they pay their median employees, an increase on stock buyback taxes and leveraging government contracts and subsidies to bar contractors from engaging in stock buybacks.

Walmart did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Sports.title: Sports Direct's Ashley attacks Burnham over 'populist' High Street revival plans
Sports.text:
Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised Prime Minister Andy Burnham's cost of living and retail policies as "populist".

In a letter to Burnham, Ashley accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons" while businesses struggled with the government's "disastrous" business rates policies and higher employment costs.

He also described a proposal to increase business rates on large warehouses in order to help reduce rates for pubs and clubs as "delusional".

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life... are affordable again"

Removing the VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms was "just the start", the government spokesperson added.

Burnham has promised to revitalise Britain's "hollowed out" High Streets and to address cost of living concerns by tackling "rip-off Britain" including misleading discounting in shops.

Ashley's Frasers Group was built on buying up struggling brands and undercutting rivals on price. It is still owned by Ashley but now run by his son-in-law Michael Murray.

The business currently owns Sports Direct, Flannels, House of Fraser, Game, Evans Cycles, Slazenger, Jack Wills, and Gieves & Hawkes, and several other retail brands.

Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times,, external hits out at the government's strategy.

"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer. You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he wrote.

He called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 28 October, to lower costs for employers and address business rates.

The government has launched a review of the tax on commercial properties, but in advance of that has already announced that pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April.

"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer-owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," Ashley's letter said.

Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty High Street properties.

Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.

The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.

In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.

The business this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.

In his letter to Burnham he asks: "My challenge to you is – how are you going to help with turning Harvey Nichols around?"

He also raises the issue of retail theft which he said cost Frasers Group approximately £40m a year.

Frasers Group has also been increasing its stake in menswear retailer Hugo Boss after its initial takeover bid for the German company was rejected.

Sports.title: Chelsea v Brighton: How the players rated
Sports.text:
Cole Palmer scored what turned out to be the decisive goal in a thrilling 4-3 victory for Chelsea over Brighton at Stamford Bridge.

Romeo Lavia, Pedro Neto and Joao Pedro put the Blues 3-0 up, but Brighton reduced the deficit to a single goal through Malick Yalcouye and a Joao Pedro own goal before Palmer made it four. Pascal Gross then headed in a 96th-minute consolation goal after a dangerous long throw-in was not dealt with.

Here's how I rated the players, and how you rated them.

Emiliano Martinez: The new signing was thrown straight in, claiming two early crosses and making saves from Malick Yalcouye and Charalampos Kostoulas - though the former did beat him with a well-struck volley. He was tested again as Brighton pushed for an equaliser in the second half. 8

Wesley Fofana: Drove forward well in possession and helped pull Brighton players out of position in the build-up. 7

Maxence Lacroix: The new signing from Crystal Palace was confident in possession but not always convincing in a defensive display that was occasionally ragged. 6

Levi Colwill: Also looked comfortable on the ball but was caught out of position at times in new manager Xabi Alonso's system. 6

Pedro Neto: Tapped in Chelsea's second goal and put a chance on a plate for Joao Pedro. However, he was most at fault for over-committing to a challenge in the build-up to Brighton's first goal. 7

Malo Gusto: Played out of position in midfield. It was a quiet performance, but he delivered some good corners. 6

Romeo Lavia: After threatening to score from a similar situation in midweek, Lavia tapped in his first Chelsea goal after four minutes. 7

Jorrel Hato: The Dutchman provided a wonderful assist on the counter-attack while playing at wing-back. 7

Cole Palmer: Scored with a wonderful curling effort in the 75th minute. He pressed well but also missed a good chance early in the second half. 8

Joao Pedro: The Brazilian produced a clever flick for Chelsea's opening goal, showcased some excellent touches and made amends for missing a good chance by scoring the Blues' third. 8

Morgan Rogers: His powerful running down the flank set up Neto for Chelsea's second goal. He should have had another assist, but Palmer blazed his effort over the bar. 7

Josh Acheampong (on 68, Fofana): Helped steady Chelsea defensively after coming on. 6

Reece James (on 68, Neto): Contributed at both ends of the pitch and provided added energy down the flank. 7

Moises Caicedo (on 68, Lavia): His afternoon was cut short after just 11 minutes as he left the pitch in tears. 6

Pep Chavarria (on 72, Colwill): An energetic cameo and looked eager to get forward. 6

Valentin Barco (on 82, Caicedo): 6

Subs not used: Penders, Gittens, Estevao Willian, Welbeck.

Sports.title: Arsenal transfer news: Gabriel Jesus close to joining Barcelona
Sports.text:
Barcelona are closing in on a move for Arsenal striker Gabriel Jesus worth £8.6m (10m euros).

A deal for the Brazil international is believed to be at an advanced stage and, while the finer details still require finalising, the transfer is expected to be completed before Tuesday's deadline.

Napoli had shown an interest in Jesus, but the 29-year-old is set to join last season's Spanish league champions and will travel for a medical on Monday.

Jesus joined Arsenal from Manchester City in 2022, scoring 32 goals and adding 22 assists in 123 appearances for the Gunners.

Speaking to the media on Thursday, Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta confirmed that Jesus was not training with the squad before Monday's Premier League game against Aston Villa (20:00 BST).

When asked whether that meant Jesus was leaving, Arteta said: "Personal situations, whatever they are, I think it's clear."

Jesus would be Barcelona's third signing from a Premier League club this summer, following the arrivals of Anthony Gordon from Newcastle and Rodri from Manchester City.

Earlier this week, Barcelona's pursuit of Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez - also an Arsenal target - appeared to end as sources told BBC Sport that Atletico would not negotiate with their Spanish rivals.

Meanwhile, Arsenal winger Gabriel Martinelli is set to travel to Saudi Arabia on Tuesday for a medical with Al-Hilal.

It is believed a deal of at least £50m has been agreed for the 25-year-old Brazil international, after Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made clear he is not in his plans.

It is understood Martinelli will sign a four-year contract, with Al-Hilal offering wages thought to be significantly more than his reported £180,000 per week deal at Arsenal.

It looked as though Barcelona were not planning to sign another striker in the event of failing to capture Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid, who continue to make a deal extremely difficult.

However, the unexpected availability of Gabriel Jesus has changed Barca's approach. The Brazilian was not initially part of the club's plans, but the circumstances surrounding his situation at Arsenal have opened the door to a move.

Barcelona have taken advantage of the fact that he is no longer as prominent in Arsenal's squad as he has been, especially with Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres now ahead of him in the pecking order.

With Jesus' Arsenal contract running until the summer of 2027, the club are willing to consider his departure for a fee rather than losing him on a free transfer next year.

The main question surrounding the move to Barca is Jesus' injury history. He has suffered significant knee problems during his time at Arsenal. An anterior cruciate ligament injury to his left knee, suffered in January 2025, kept him out for 10 months.

None of these necessarily means Barcelona will abandon their long-term interest in Alvarez.

Following Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres' departures from the club, Barcelona wanted to add a natural centre-forward to their attacking options. Jesus offers something different from a traditional number nine, with his ability to operate across the front line and contribute to the build-up making him an attractive option for Hansi Flick.

If the deal is completed, Flick will be adding a highly experienced forward to his squad. Jesus made 27 appearances for Arsenal last season in all competitions, scoring six goals, while his six-season spell at Manchester City produced 236 appearances and 95 goals.

For Barca, the move represents a relatively low-cost opportunity to add experience, versatility and Premier League pedigree to their attack.

Sports.title: US Open 2026 singles preview: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz fare on comeback?
Sports.text:
All was bright in Aryna Sabalenka's world when she completed a rare 'Sunshine Double' earlier this season.

Becoming only the fifth woman to win the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back, Sabalenka emphasised her position as the dominant player on the WTA Tour and created a 3,000-point lead at the top of the world rankings.

But a difficult period quickly followed - seemingly out of nowhere - leaving the 28-year-old Belarusian clinging on to her position going into the US Open, which starts on Sunday.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka returns to New York with a 17-7 win-loss record since the Miami triumph, including a chastening French Open quarter-final exit and a disheartening defeat in the Wimbledon fourth round.

It is a record far below the four-time major winner's lofty standards.

With 2,000 points to defend at Flushing Meadows and Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina now trailing by only 434, Sabalenka must win again to extend her 99-week run as the world number one.

Asked if she felt confident she can rediscover her mojo on the hard courts on which she has thrived, Sabalenka said: "Absolutely. These tough lessons are definitely going to make me way, way stronger and working even harder."

Sabalenka's four Grand Slam singles titles - two Australian Open and two US Open triumphs, all on hard courts - are more than most players can dream of.

However, she has also lost four major finals and six semi-finals, despite a consistency on the biggest stages that is unrivalled among her peers.

The concern in recent months has been Sabalenka's mental focus disappearing in less pressurised situations.

This was most recently apparent in her Cincinnati Open fourth-round defeat by 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek. Sabalenka led 5-1 in a first-set tie-break and 4-1 in the second set, but continued to lack composure in the rallies as Bejlek rallied to win 7-6 (9-7) 6-4.

At her previous tournament in Toronto, she lost to Russian world number 19 Ekaterina Alexandrova in the last 16 as her serve crumbled.

During the clay-court swing, Sabalenka capitulated after winning the first set against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid, Sorana Cirstea in Rome and, most notably, Diana Shnaider at Roland Garros.

"I work on my mental side of the game. I've been trying to reset my mind and to come back stronger," a bullish Sabalenka said in New York.

"It's only a matter of time for me to come back."

The drop-off in Sabalenka's results have opened the door for Rybakina, who beat the Belarusian to win the Australian Open in January, to take over as world number one.

Rybakina might not even have to win a match at Flushing Meadows to do that, as she has fewer ranking points to defend than Sabalenka.

However, there are questions over her fitness because of an ankle injury sustained in the Cincinnati quarter-finals.

Rybakina can secure the number one ranking if her nearest rivals - Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - do not win the title.

If Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still also rise to the top by reaching the semi-finals.

Pegula, 32, has been ultra-consistent for several seasons without landing a major title, but the 2024 finalist hopes her runs to the Washington and Cincinnati finals will provide the platform for another crack at her home Slam.

Gauff, who beat Pegula to the Cincinnati trophy last week, already has the experience of winning in New York after claiming her first major there in 2023.

Twelve months ago, the 22-year-old American's game was clouded by uncertainty but returns with more confidence and fluidity in her serve.

Beneath the leading quartet, the rest of the top 10 also hold either a Grand Slam or WTA 1,000 title - a group led by French Open winner Mirra Andreeva, Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and six-time major winner Iga Swiatek.

"You can just see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.

The Serb great, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, insists he has not put an "expiry date" on his extraordinary career. He continues to put himself in the mix for titles as he looks to finally land a standalone record 25th victory which would move him clear of Australia's Margaret Court on the all-time list.

He has reached at least the semi-finals in six of the past seven Slams, but has not gone all the way since triumphing at the 2023 US Open.

Germany's Alexander Zverev leads the seedings as he looks to reach a third straight major final, having won his first Slam at the French Open before losing to Sinner at Wimbledon.

Canadian Open champion Ben Shelton and Cincinnati finalist Frances Tiafoe lead a strong American challenge, while 2024 finalist Taylor Fritz is another hope capable of ending a 23-year wait for a home men's champion.

Sports.title: Mountain Bike World Championships: Tom Pidcock dedicates second title to Fin Tarling
Sports.text:
Great Britain's Tom Pidcock paid an emotional tribute to Fin Tarling after winning his second cross-country world title at the Mountain Bike World Championships in Val di Sole, Italy.

British cyclist Tarling, 19, died after an accident during the Volta a Portugal earlier this month.

Pidcock, a two-time Olympic champion, said: "I want to dedicate this win to Fin Tarling and Josh [Tarling] - seeing him start the Vuelta was pretty incredible.

"I want to dedicate this to him and his family."

The 27-year-old, who won mountain bike gold at the Paris Olympics, added to his 2023 world title that he won in Scotland.

Having been a last-minute entrant after finishing ninth in this year's Tour de France, Pidcock finished 17 seconds clear of Great Britain team-mate Charlie Aldridge - who took his second silver of the championships - with Canada's Cole Punchard third.

Pidcock accelerated clear of Aldridge on lap seven of eight, riding clear before embracing the crowd and lifting up his bike at the finish line in a time of one hour 25 minutes and 26 seconds.

"I crashed pretty badly in practice on Friday and my back was hurting from the first lap. The last two laps I just had to push and stretch that gap before a final sprint. That was a pretty hard race," he added.

Switzerland's Sina Frei won the women's cross-country title, with Great Britain's Evie Richards crossing in sixth place.

On Thursday Richards, 29, narrowly missed out on a second elite women's short track world title as she was edged into second on the line by Austria's Laura Stigger.

Having rounded the final corner in the lead, Richards faded as Stigger came on her left to take the title by little more than a wheel rim.

Aldridge also picked up silver on Thursday in the elite men's short track.

The 25-year-old looked in control on the long final straight but France's Adrien Boichis pipped him to gold.

In the downhill on Saturday, Great Britain's Harriet Harnden claimed bronze in the women's event and Jordan Williams did the same in the men's.

Sports.title: British Masters golf: England's Joe Dean storms to title with stunning round at The Belfry
Sports.text:
British Masters final leaderboard

-14 J Dean (Eng); -11 JS Olesen (Den), N Norgaard (Den), N Elvira (Spa), D Hillier (NZ)

Selected: -10 M Penge (Eng), T McKibbin (NI); -9 F Zanotti (Par); -8 M Wallace (Eng), E Ferguson (Sco)

Former supermarket delivery driver Joe Dean fired a sensational bogey-free nine-under-par 63 to snatch the British Masters title at The Belfry.

It is a first DP World Tour victory in his 70th event for the 32-year-old Englishman who is ranked 292nd in the world.

He collected the trophy and about £440,000 in prize money, more than he had earned in total from his previous 19 tournaments in the 2026 season.

"All those painful hours and all the work, it's finally led to something," said Dean, who two years ago was delivering groceries to help fund his golf.

"It was a rare day when everything felt right and the putts were dropping and I couldn't do anything wrong."

It caps a busy summer for the Sheffield golfer who won the inaugural Last Chance Qualifier on the Monday of Open Championship week in July to earn the final spot in the field at Royal Birkdale.

He then married Emily, who carried his bag that week and this.

"I can't thank her enough," said Dean on Sky Sports. "I hope I made her proud."

Dean started Sunday's final round seven shots behind leader Dan Hillier and made a move with four birdies in his opening six holes. Five more followed on the back nine, including a 10-footer at the last to set the target at 14 under par.

He then had to wait about 90 minutes to be crowned champion as challengers came and faded.

Dean eventually won by three strokes from four players, including 2023 champion Hillier, at a tournament that was disrupted by stormy conditions in Warwickshire.

More than nine hours of play was lost on Thursday and Friday, leaving organisers scrambling to complete the event before more forecast inclement weather returned.

Marco Penge, who had a breakthrough year in 2025 with three wins, led on 10 under after a sparkling 65 in round two.

He also started the final round on that total after completing a third-round 72 on Sunday morning.

Five birdies and two bogeys in his first nine holes of round four catapulted Penge into a one-stroke lead with nine to play.

However, a third bogey of the round, on the 11th, halted his momentum and five more pars followed to leave him 12 under with two to play.

Penge compounded the error of a wild drive into trees on the par-five 17th by hitting a branch with his second shot and then had to chip out sideways with his third.

That led to a bogey and with his challenge over, he dropped a shot at the last too to finish with a 72 and 10-under total.

A double-bogey six on the sixth hurt Hillier's tilt at winning a second title. And while the New Zealander had two birdies on his back nine, he closed with a one-over 73 to finish on 11 under.

That left him joint second alongside the Danish pair of Niklas Norgaard and Jacob Skov Olesen who both signed for 71s, and Spain's Nacho Elvira who carded a 69.

Paraguay's Fabrizio Zanotti threatened to trouble Dean's lead late on after firing four birdies in five holes during a purple patch on his back nine to get to 12 under, but he had a triple bogey on the last after taking two shots to get out of a fairway bunker and then finding water.

The British Masters was the first event in the race to qualify for the European team to take on the United States at next year's Ryder Cup in Ireland.

Sports.title: Harrison Armstrong: Everton call off transfer to Nottingham Forest after fan backlash
Sports.text:
Everton have called off a proposed deal to sell midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest following a backlash from the club's supporters.

Forest made a bid of £40m plus a potential sell-on clause for the England Under-19 international, who is regarded as one of the brightest prospects to emerge from Finch Farm in recent years.

The news enraged Everton supporters, who sang Armstrong's name throughout Saturday's draw at Bournemouth and said there would be a "riot" if he was sold.

Everton's board, led by chair Dan Friedkin, eventually decided to reject Forest's bid – with the owner at the forefront of the discussions.

Armstrong has made 24 appearances for Everton and played 87 minutes against the Cherries before he was replaced by Charly Alcaraz.

Speaking after the game Toffees boss David Moyes said he understood the fans' frustration and appeared to suggest the decision was out of his hands.

"I think you always have to consider supporters; supporters aren't always wrong," Moyes.

"But then there are also times where I've had people at clubs who are really powerful and make difficult decisions.

"Managers have to make decisions on players sometimes and they feel like huge decisions. But there are sometimes bigger decisions to be made and the club will, I'm sure, make what they think is the right one.

"If I'd say something to them (the fans), I'd say their manager's an Evertonian."

Moyes has been frustrated by the club's lack of signings and he made it clear he wanted reinforcements after the Carabao Cup second-round win against Preston on Wednesday.

The Toffees have signed Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough for an initial £16m and fellow midfielder Christian Norgaard from Arsenal for £7m

Tyrique George and Merlin Rohl signed permanent deals after loan spells last season, while Brennan Johnson joined from Crystal Palace in a swap deal with Dwight McNeil.

Shortly after the Armstrong news broke it emerged that Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Toffees forward Iliman Ndiaye, with Richarlison set to return to Merseyside in a separate deal.

Talks are ongoing and moving forward between Everton and Manchester City for Jack Grealish to return before the deadline, with another loan the most likely option at this stage.

However, the club have yet to sign a right-back to replace Seamus Coleman, though they have revived interest in Kenny Tete, who turned down the Toffees to sign a new deal at Fulham last year.

Everton's decision to reject Nottingham Forest's offer for teenager Harrison Armstrong has headed off the possibility of open revolt against owners The Friedkin Group from a furious fanbase.

The revelation that Everton had received a £40m bid from Forest for the gifted 19-year-old, and it was under consideration, sparked an instant backlash from fans angry at the idea the club's best homegrown product for years could be sold.

Instead, after a day of drama on and off the field, Everton's board - led by chairman and billionaire owner Dan Friedkin - decided to unanimously reject Forest's approach and keep Armstrong.

Everton's fans made their feelings clear during the 1-1 draw at Bournemouth. The reaction was so loud, and toxic, that it is sure to have been heard by Everton's delegation at The Vitality Stadium and relayed back to the hierarchy in the United States.

It is highly unlikely to be coincidence that a deal that looked to be advancing was then stopped in its tracks.

And it will also pacify manager David Moyes, whose mood looked ominous post-match at Bournemouth, as he will now keep a young talent regarded as a key part of the club's future.

Everton's supporters may reluctantly accept that important players could be prised away by Champions League clubs, but the notion of Nottingham Forest being able to do the same added another layer to their fury.

Forest are one of the club's Everton and their fans would hope to surpass, not bolster them by selling one of their crown jewels to them.

For The Friedkin Group, it is a PR catastrophe avoided.

It has been a remarkable 24 hours that has seen Everton supporters unite to keep one of their rising stars.

Armstrong is seen as a beacon of light in what has been a barren period for the club's academy set up. The 19-year-old scouser is so highly regarded that he has been touted as a future club captain.

The travelling Toffees sang throughout the 90 minutes at Bournemouth, sending a message that they wanted their rising talent to stay. Captain James Tarkowski and Moyes also made it clear in their post-match interviews they were against any sale.

The fans group The 1878s, who organise pre-match fan and banner displays at Hill Dickinson Stadium, put out a strong statement saying they were ready to step down from their role if Armstrong was sold.

What owners the Friedkin Group have seen is a display of unity they may not have expected.

Sports.title: Tottenham transfer news: Spurs advancing move for Iliman Ndiaye with Richarlison set to rejoin Everton
Sports.text:
Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction as part of separate negotiations.

Although a deal for Ndiaye is largely agreed between the two clubs, it remains unclear whether he will make the switch to north London, with Manchester City among the clubs to have expressed an interest.

City have also held talks to sign Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, another Spurs target, although the Reds would need to secure a replacement before sanctioning any move.

Everton are open to selling Ndiaye, 26, after he rejected multiple contract offers and held talks with Saudi club Al-Hilal earlier this summer.

Meanwhile, Everton have agreed terms in principle to re-sign striker Richarlison after he told Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi "too many times that he wants to leave".

The Brazil international has entered the final year of his Tottenham contract and would provide competition for first-choice striker Thierno Barry, with uncertainty surrounding Beto's future at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Everton are also growing increasingly confident of completing a loan deal to bring Jack Grealish back from Manchester City, although the precise terms of any agreement remain complicated as the England international enters the final year of his contract at Etihad Stadium.

Grealish has prioritised a return to Everton, where he spent last season on loan, over the option of rejoining his boyhood club Aston Villa, who have also expressed an interest.

Everton are also targeting a right-back and are close to agreeing a £9m deal for Fulham's Kenny Tete, who came close to joining last summer.

Fulham are already assessing potential replacements and have entered talks to sign Rayo Vallecano's Andrei Ratiu.

It is part of a chain of interconnected Premier League deals before Tuesday's transfer deadline.

Richarlison is one of three players who De Zerbi says have asked to leave Tottenham.

He, Kevin Danso and Pape Matar Sarr have all been linked with moves away from Spurs and none were included in De Zerbi's match squad as Tottenham lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle on Saturday.

Asked about their status after the loss, De Zerbi said: "Richarlison, I don't know. He said too many times he wants to leave.

"Danso came to me two days ago and he said wants to leave and Pape Sarr the same, but he suffered a small injury, but he is almost ready to train.

"I have very good relationships but if they want to leave, they have to bring the solution, the economic solution, to the club, and they can go."

Spurs have spent more than £300m this summer in an effort to restore their competitive edge following back-to-back 17th-place Premier League finishes.

But Tottenham are bottom of the table, having lost their first two games to Brentford and Newcastle and failing to score a goal.

With 11 goals, Richarlison was Tottenham's top scorer last season and a key figure during their struggle for Premier League survival, which was secured on the final day.

Earlier in August, De Zerbi said that the Brazilian was uncertain about his future, noting that "it's not easy to find another striker like Richarlison".

Last week, Manchester City striker Omar Marmoush joined Spurs on loan and he replaced Richarlison in De Zerbi's starting XI against Newcastle.

Danso's first-team opportunities may be limited this season as Marcos Senesi and Jan Paul van Hecke arrive to challenge for his place in central defence, where Micky van de Ven's spot was secured by the signing of a new contract and the award of the captaincy.

Sunderland made an offer to take Danso, who has 36 Austria caps, on a season-long loan - but Spurs rejected it.

In midfield, Sarr's chance to play has been impacted by the arrivals of Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali early in the window, as Tottenham kicked off their a statement summer of transfers by breaking their club record fee twice in one week.

The Senegal international, 23, has attracted interest from a number of clubs, including several in the Premier League and Turkish side Besiktas.

However, Juventus are understood to be confident of winning the race for his signature on a loan deal that includes a conditional obligation to buy.

Sports.title: King Charles: Pakistan to meet King following controversial Lord's Test
Sports.text:
Pakistan will have an audience with King Charles this week, days after a threat to cancel their tour of England was made because of an interview with the sons of Imran Khan.

During lunch on day one of the second Test, Sky Sports aired an interview with Suleiman and Kasim Khan, the sons of former Pakistan captain and prime minister Imran.

Imran Khan has been in prison for the past three years on charges of corruption, which he denies.

Before the interview was aired, the Pakistan Cricket Board raised the prospect of not resuming the second Test at Lord's and cancelling the remainder of the three-match series.

At the time, the England and Wales Cricket Board took government advice from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

Buckingham Palace has confirmed the King is expected to meet the tourists later this week in an engagement planned before the series began.

"His Majesty the King, as Head of the Commonwealth, will receive the Pakistan Men's Test Cricket Team for an audience in the gardens of Clarence House, in the break between the second and third Test matches hosted in England over the summer," said a statement.

It is understood His Majesty will spend around 15 minutes with the Pakistan team.

Legendary all-rounder Imran Khan, 73, had a 21-year international career for Pakistan and famously led his team to World Cup glory in 1992.

He served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022 and was jailed a year later.

In December of last year, Imran Khan's sister appealed to King Charles in his position of head of the Commonwealth to speak out on the situation.

According to The Times, Aleema Khanum said: "Pakistan is a member of the Commonwealth of Nations.

"Its key principles in the charter are rule of law, democracy, and human rights. A member nation is busy destroying all three fundamental principles.

"Member states, especially where King Charles is the head of the Commonwealth organisation, don't speak out against fascism or military dictatorship? What is the point of just organisations then?"

The chairman of the PCB, Mohsin Naqvi, serves as interior minister for the current Pakistan government. The PCB has been contacted for confirmation Naqvi will be present for the audience with the King.

Before the interview with Khan's sons aired, Sky received a complaint, yet pressed ahead with airing a version of former England captain Michael Atherton's conversation with Suleiman and Kasim.

In the interview, Suleiman and Kasim expressed concerns over the treatment and security given to their father, as well as criticising the UK government's response.

Despite the controversy caused by the interview, the Pakistan team returned to the field as scheduled after lunch on the opening day of the second Test.

At the close of play on the second day, Pakistan coach Sarfaraz Ahmed said he and his team did not know about the interview.

"I don't know anything. I'm just focusing on the match," said Sarfaraz. "You're talking about the interview? We don't know about the interview."

In October, England will tour Pakistan for a one-day tri-series against the home side and Sri Lanka.

It will be England's fourth separate tour of Pakistan in the past four years following a 17-year gap between visits to the country because of security concerns.

Sports.title: Dragons' Den offers Peterborough street artist advice - and a job
Sports.text:
A street artist who appeared on the BBC Dragons' Den came away with an offer of both professional advice - and a job.

Nathan Murdoch, 38, runs Street Arts Hire and has painted several murals in Peterborough, including tributes to Prodigy singer Keith Flint, and a Jude Bellingham portrait during the football World Cup.

He said he went on the show looking for further investment in his arts business, but all the Dragons agreed instead that he needed sound advice in order to expand.

Entrepreneur Steven Bartlett was so taken with Murdoch's work he offered the artist both one-to-one advice and a job painting the walls of his new London offices.

Murdoch appeared before the entrepreneurs accompanied by a large painting of a dragon - which he had created for the show.

He was asking for a £60,000 investment in return for a 10% share in his company.

The money, he said, would help employ a full-time role co-ordinating the work he and other artists were commissioned to do, as he said they could only currently fill about 60% of requests.

Murdoch is well known in Peterborough and in February he hosted an exhibition, Diesel Streets, celebrating more than two decades of graffiti and the city's street art culture.

The quality of his art stunned all five Dragons on the show, which aired on 27 August on BBC One.

Looking at the dragon painting brought in by Murdoch, Bartlett said: "You make me feel like a muggle just looking at that, thinking that a human being could do that versus what I can do. It's incredible."

Gary Neville said: "The artwork is absolutely stunning. You're taking home only £30,000 a year but you're a creative, you're a genius."

Pointing at the painting, which took Murdoch four hours to create, he said: "That's worth thousands of pounds", and quipped he would pay £5,000 for it.

Sports.title: Manchester United v Ipswich Town: Premier League – live
Sports.text:
38 min Fernandes tries a short-corner routine but messes it up by passing straight to a defender. Rashford manages a cross, only to see it gobbled up by the giant Scherpen.

37 min Another foul, and it’s an ugly one. Fatawu goes sliding in on Mbeumo and gets a booking. He may be in trouble with the Union of Right-Wingers too.

36 min Ipswich, by the way, haven’t won at Old Trafford since 1984.

35 min United’s turn to commit a gratuitous foul as Harry Maguire manhandles Emersonn near the halfway line. Tielemans is then caught napping, but United see off the danger.

34 min Sasa Lukic, who’s been a big presence in midfield, brings down Tielemans when he doesn’t need to, and gets a yellow card.

33 min The cameras find Michael Carrick looking pensive, as well he may. Are United disintegrating again in the face of a promoted team with a bit of spirit?

31 min Chance for Ipswich: Davis again! It’s another fine cross from Fatawu. Davis, perhaps surprised to find himself getting all these openings, shoots a bit limply at point-blank range.

GOAL! Man United 0-1 Ipswich (Davis 29)

It’s last weekend all over again! Fatawu surges down the right wing, shrugs off Shaw and crosses to Davis, whose finish goes in off the bar.

Updated at 12.06 EDT

28 min Another minute, another United attack. Mbeumo curls in a cross from the right which is just too high for Fernandes and Rashford, coming in at the far post.

27 min “United’s midfield were criticised for not being positive enough last week,” Gary Neville says, “and they’ve been better here, Mainoo and Fernandes linking well.”

26 min Fernandes takes it himself and hits it into the wall.

25 min United spring forward andf again Ipswich resort to a foul as Maeda trips Cunha. This free kick is five yards closer than the last one.

24 min It’s been a lovely open game with the crowd in good voice. But they may get antsy soon, as United still haven’t scored this season.

23 min More xG for Ipswich! Leif Davis flies down the left, collects a pinpoint through ball and sees his shot well saved by Lammens.

20 min United have had six shots, Ipswich only one (that tame one from Maeda evidently didn’t trouble the scorers), but when the xG flashed up just now, it was 0.34-0.23 to the Tractor Boys.

20 min Fernandes leaves the free kick to Rashford, who has scored with a free kick in El Clasico since he was last seen at Old Trafford. He hits it well but just over.

19 min Kobbie Mainoo has started brightly too. He wins a free kick about 30 yards out in the middle.

18 min Martinez, recalled partly for his passing, sends a piercing ball to Shaw, who is very well tackled by Jacob Greaves.

16 min Fernandes looks himself again after a couple of flat performances (and two missed pens). But the other No 10, Enciso, looks just as incisive.

16 min Shaw’s through ball finds Fernandes, who can’t quite bring it under control. It turns out he was offside anyway.

14 min Big chance for Ipswich! They break from the corner and Enciso holds off Shaw and Mbeumo to get a shot away, well saved by Lammens. Then the ball goes up the other end, where Rashford is inches away from sliding in to meet Cunha’s low cross.

12 min Save! By Scherpen from Dalot, who curled a classy left-foot shot towards the top corner. It was a flowing move from United that involved both wingers.

11 min Ipswich attack again. As a cross comes in from the left, Martinez can’t reach it and Shaw has to bail him out with a header.

7 min Maeda sees that run and more than matches it, tearing down the left and landing the first shot on target, which is too tame to trouble Lammens.

Updated at 11.42 EDT

6 min Cunha passes to Rashford, who goes on a slalom before returning the compliment. Cunha’s shot is always going over.

6 min The first shot is taken by … Rashford, from distance, but it’s half-blocked by an Ipswich foot and loops up kindly for Scherpen, the giant in their goal.

5 min United pass the ball around at the back before Martinez hits it out. Gary O’Neil must have been tempted to play a back five, after seeing United struggle to cope with Hull’s wing-backs, but it seems to be a back four .

4 min Rashford has now gone more minutes without a goal today than he did when he last faced Ipswich: he scored after 2 min in Ruben Amorim’s first game as manager, which ended in a draw.

3 min As expected, Carrick has Mbeumo on the right, Mbeumo in the middle and Rashford on the left. Rashford makes his first run now, but is well marshalled by O’Shea I think.

1 min Ipswich kick off, head over to their right and run into Luke Shaw, who bundles the ball out. They’re in off-white with black shorts: have they borrowed United’s third kit?

Lisandro Martinez lost only one game of the 13 he started last season, apparently. Fun fact: he’s not the only Argentinian here with a World Cup medal – Exequiel Palacios has just joined Ipswich and he’s on the bench.

Out come the players, some of them holding babes in arms – including Marcus Rashford, who has a big smile on his face.

The first email of the afternoon comes from Dave. “Hi Tim, loving the MBM.” Thanks! “Just wondered if there’s any insight into why Sesko seems to find it so hard to get a start.”

At the moment he’s coming back from injury – he was understandably rusty when he came on for the last half-hour at Hull. But it’s true that Carrick has sometimes had him on the bench by choice. There was a spell in the new year when Sesko was United’s best super-sub since Ole Gunnar Solskjaer.

A bit of change at Old Trafford, too. The turf has been relaid, for the first time in 14 years. So not even Luke Shaw was there when it last happened.

Here’s Gary O’Neil, being asked about Ipswich’s fine start against Sunderland. “It gave everyone a nice boost,” he says. “Lot of change, obviously… This is a real tough test for us, but one that the group are ready for. We’ve worked really hard over the past eight weeks.”

It’s full time in the 2pm games. Chelsea have beaten Brighton 4-3 in a game that wasn’t quite as close as it sounds. Leeds and Brentford have drawn 1-1, and Sunderland have bucked the trend I mentioned by beating Fulham 1-0 after losing last weekend.

So Fulham join Palace, Coventry and Spurs on nul points after two games, while Chelsea emulate Man City and the mighty Hull in starting with successive wins. Do join John Brewin for more.

Updated at 11.07 EDT

How bad were United last weekend? The result was a shocker, and so was the defending at set pieces –but they didn’t concede in open play, did create plenty of chances and led their manager to say that they “did some good things”. For United Writing, the free microsite I run with Rob Smyth, I tried to weigh up the good, the bad and the ugly.

It will be interesting to see how United’s front three line up. Bryan Mbeumo started most of the pre-season games at centre-forward and was probably United’s best player, along with Mason Mount. But because Amad had to pull out of the Hull game with injury, Mbeumo went back to the right wing, and Matheus Cunha started as a deep-lying, if not quite false, 9. Rashford has played more often in the middle for United than either of them, but the chances are that he’ll start on the left, where he offers more width (and pace) than Cunha.

Updated at 10.48 EDT

Teams in full: four changes for United, none for Ipswich

Gary O’Neil reverts to his first XI and sees no reason to change a winning team.

Man United (4-2-3-1) Lammens; Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw; Tielemans, Mainoo; Mbeumo, Fernandes, Rashford; Cunha.

Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, Yoro, Martinez, Santos, Lacey, Zirkzee, Dorgu, Sesko.

Ipswich (4-2-3-1) Scherpen; O’Shea, Diop, Greaves, Davis; Nunez, Lukic; Fatawu, Enciso, Maeda; Emersonn.

Subs: Walton, Furlong, Egeli, Kipre, Palacios, Ouattara, McAteer, Clarke, Akpom.

Rashford starts!

Marcus Rashford, who came on at half-time last weekend and played more key passes in 45 minutes than Bruno Fernandes managed in 90, is rewarded with his first start since he was frozen out by Ruben Amorim in December 2024. He replaces Patrick Dorgu on the left. Michael Carrick also shakes up his defence, bringing in Diogo Dalot and Lisandro Martinez, and in midfield Andrey Santos gives way to Kobbie Mainoo.

Updated at 10.24 EDT

Afternoon everyone and welcome to the Arnold Mühren derby. It’s a game that looms larger now than it did before the season began. Then, it seemed like a surprising choice for the Sunday-teatime slot, but since last weekend it has looked rather shrewd. Ipswich hit the ground running with a win over Sunderland, while Manchester United slipped on a banana skin at Hull.

Michael Carrick still has his proud record of winning two-thirds of his matches as United boss (in both his stints). And one of the things his team did well last season was bouncing back from disappointment. After losing at Newcastle, they beat Villa at Old Trafford; after losing to Leeds at home, they went to Chelsea and won.

Gary O’Neil, though, has a 100pc record as manager of Ipswich – played two, won two. He made nine changes for the League Cup game against Leicester and still emerged with a 3-1 win. His first XI, now featuring Julio Enciso and Sasa Lukic, come to Old Trafford with nothing to lose.

As I write this, at half-time in the 2pm games, no club in the Premier League have lost their first match of the season and won their second (or taken the lead today). Can United change that? They badly need to, with a Manchester derby looming and an October fixture list that includes trips to Atletico Madrid, Leeds, Como and Chelsea.

For Ipswich, it’s the first of three games against the big names in 17 days. The other two are at Portman Road: Liverpool in the league on Friday and Arsenal in the Carabao Cup on 15 September. So this is just a warm-up.

Back soon with the teams.

Updated at 10.14 EDT

Gaming_Tech.title: Switzerland rave shooting kills woman, 22 as manhunt launched
Gaming_Tech.text:
A manhunt is under way after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five others injured in a shooting at a rave in Switzerland.

The woman died at the scene in Aarau, police said. Four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were in hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe".

Sources have confirmed to BBC News that the victim was an Italian national. The Italian Embassy in Bern and the Consulate in Zurich were monitoring the situation, they added.

At a news conference on Sunday afternoon, police spokesman Bernhard Graser reiterated the force had "no information about the perpetrator(s) or their motive". They were not believed to be in Aarau anymore, he added.

Organisers and performers said the shooting happened at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in the town, which is located some 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich.

The force said it had received an initial report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at around 02:30 local time (00:30 GMT).

A DJ, who was due to perform until the scheduled end of the event at 02:00, said the incident occurred "straight after our set", in a post on social media.

Another performer, DJ Tekibo, said he had lost a friend in the incident. He wrote on Instagram that he was "still trying to process what happened".

Olivier Grein, whose firm Agency Events AG organised the event, said the company was "shaken" and would do all it could to support the police investigation.

An eyewitness told Blick that he "suddenly heard the gunshots" minutes after the music stopped at 02:30, initially believing they were fireworks.

He said he was told to hide by a man and a woman, the latter of whom was then shot.

Organisers had expected up to 3,500 people to attend. Police asked witnesses to submit photographs and video from the scene.

Gaming_Tech.title: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge says
Gaming_Tech.text:
A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless".

The company argued in the lawsuit that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority with the new designation. It followed Anthropic's refusal to allow the military to use its AI models for tasks including surveillance or autonomous weapons.

US District Judge Rita Lin said in the ruling that citing national security was "not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics".

Anthropic welcomed the ruling. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon and the White House for comment.

Anthropic was focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology", a spokesperson told the BBC.

Judge Lin said in the court filing that the Defense Department had acted unlawfully to order firms that do business with the US military to boycott Anthropic.

The Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk in February - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.

It marked the first time an American company had been publicly designated as such.

Anthropic's lawsuit said the government's actions were both "unprecedented and unlawful".

The Claude maker said its models were not reliable enough to be safely used in weapons systems for the military. It added that it opposed its use for domestic surveillance as a violation of rights.

The Pentagon said at the time that private companies should not be able to constrain military action.

The White House had previously said Anthropic was "a radical left, woke company attempting to control military activity" and argued the military was beholden to the US Constitution, "not any woke AI company's terms of service".

The Pentagon also argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over what the company could do with its technology.

Anthropic said in its lawsuit that its business had been impacted by the government's actions and its right to freedom of speech had been violated.

Judge Lin said during an earlier round in the lawsuit that the government was trying to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI.

"This appears to be classic First Amendment retaliation," the judge added.
